prompt: Why do we still say "dial" a phone number? Essay.

ok so I've been thinking about this since my dad passed. his email account is still active and every few weeks it gets a newsletter from a fishing supply store he used to order from. I can't bring myself to unsubscribe him. I'd love an essay about what happens to our digital leftovers when we die, not the legal stuff about passwords and estates, more about what it means that the internet keeps talking to people who aren't there anymore. personal-ish tone is fine, maybe 1200 words.
Make the case that the password, for all its flaws, is one of the most humane security technologies ever invented. I'm tired of hearing it's dead.
Write something exploring why every software update seems to make my phone slightly worse at the thing I actually use it for.

I'm 41 and I just ran my first sub-4 marathon after six years of trying. Everyone keeps asking what changed and honestly the answer is boring: I started running slower in training. Can you help me write a personal essay about the counterintuitive idea that getting faster mostly means going slow? I want it to feel earned, not like a training tips listicle.
Essay: why nobody watches minor league soccer but everyone watches minor league baseball.

I'd appreciate a reflective essay on the decline of the hyperlink as a form of citation in online writing, and what has replaced it: screenshots, quote-tweets, "link in bio." Around 1000 words, for a general but literate audience.

For my climbing blog: why bouldering gyms have become the new bars for people in their late twenties. I have theories (no alcohol required, built-in conversation starters, nobody looks at their phone) but want the essay to actually figure out what's going on rather than just list them.

My 9 year old asked me if Alexa is alive. I said no, but then she asked how I know and I didn't have a good answer. Could you write an essay I could maybe adapt for our school's parent newsletter about how to talk to kids about machines that talk back? I don't want it preachy.

I'm a physical therapist. Write an op-ed arguing that the "no pain no gain" mindset has been replaced by an equally unhelpful opposite: people so afraid of injury they never load their tissues enough to get stronger. Should be pointed but fair, ~800 words, aimed at regular gym-goers rather than clinicians.
why spreadsheets are underrated as a creative medium. go

What I wish I knew about building a personal website at 15 that I only figured out at 35. Write it as a personal essay. Context: I had a Geocities page with a guestbook and a hit counter, and I think it taught me more about the web than my CS degree.
Is the marathon actually a good distance for humans or just a historical accident we've turned into a bucket list item? Write it up as an essay. I lean toward "accident" but convince me either way.
Write an essay questioning whether "screen time" is even a meaningful category anymore. Reading a novel on a Kindle, video calling grandma, and doomscrolling all count the same, which seems absurd.
short essay on the strange intimacy of the locker room

As someone who's maintained an open source library for 11 years with roughly 4 million weekly downloads and zero pay, I want an essay about the moral economy of open source: who owes what to whom. Not a rant about corporations freeloading (I've read a hundred of those). I'm more interested in the obligations that run the other way, what maintainers owe users, and whether "I don't owe you anything" is actually true.
Write a mock-serious essay defending the walk-off as the most dramatically perfect ending in all of sport, better than the buzzer-beater, better than penalties.
Why do people trust a restaurant with 4.6 stars and 2,000 reviews more than one with 5.0 and 12? I know the stats answer but I want an essay about what star ratings have done to how we decide things.

I lost about 70 pounds over two years and the weirdest part isn't the body, it's that I still see the old one. I walk sideways through doorways I'd easily fit through. I'd love an essay about how slowly the mind updates its map of the body. Not a weight loss story, more about proprioception and identity.
Compose an essay on the ethics of reading someone's old public posts, say, a job candidate's tweets from 2013. Is the past of the internet fair game?
Why do runners hate treadmills? Essay please.

I work in IT support for a mid-sized law firm and the single most common ticket I get is someone who "lost" a file they saved to their desktop. Not because they're dumb, these are very smart lawyers. I've started to think the whole folder/file metaphor just doesn't match how people's brains work anymore, especially for anyone who grew up with search and phones. could you write an essay on whether the file system is a dying idea? Something I might post on my LinkedIn without it being cringe.
Argue that youth sports would be better if we stopped keeping score until age 12. Then, in the same essay, take that argument apart honestly. I coach U10 and genuinely don't know where I land.
An essay on the CAPTCHA: a test we take dozens of times a month to prove something about ourselves that is getting harder and harder to prove.

Write a personal essay in my voice about playing pickup basketball at the same park for 20 years and watching the regulars change. I'm 52, the court got resurfaced last spring and somehow that's what made me want to write about it.
Op-ed, maybe 700 words: the group chat has quietly replaced the town square, the dinner party and the family phone call, and nobody voted for that.
What is it about stretching? Every coach swears by it, every study seems to say it barely matters, and I still feel better when I do it. Write an essay that tries to untangle this.

I teach high school English. I'd like an essay arguing that autocomplete, not cheating, is the real threat to how teenagers learn to write, because it teaches them to accept the most likely next word. ~1000 words, thoughtful not alarmist.
Blog post essay: why I quit my fitness tracker after 6 years and 2.1 million logged steps, and what I noticed about my body once the numbers were gone.
the case for dumb TVs
Why is it that in almost every sport the left-handers are overrepresented at the top? Explore what that tells us about competition, not just biology.

I'm the person in my family everyone calls for tech help. My mom, my uncle, two neighbors. It's sweet but also exhausting and it's changed my relationships in ways I didn't expect. write an essay about being the family's tech support, the strange power and resentment of it

I would like an essay on the ethics of spectator sports that knowingly damage the athletes' brains: American football, boxing, and to a lesser extent soccer heading. What does it mean to enjoy watching that?
Write about why the humble QR code had the greatest comeback story in tech history. It was a joke in 2012 and then the pandemic happened.

I'm 34 and just started powerlifting. Everyone at the gym is either 22 or a 60-year-old who's been doing it forever. Could you write an essay about starting something physical "too late," what you lose and what you might actually gain by not having started at 18? Honest, not a pep talk.
Is "the algorithm" actually a thing, or have we invented a convenient villain to explain why we spend our evenings the way we do? Write it up as an essay.
An essay on golf as the only sport where you're expected to call penalties on yourself, and what that says about which games produce honest people.
Write a personal-essay-style piece about the moment the internet stopped feeling like a place you go and started feeling like the weather.

Ex-D1 swimmer here, now 29. I'd love an essay on what happens to elite athletes' identities in the year after they retire, written for a general audience. I have firsthand material: I didn't swim a single lap for 14 months and gained a weird kind of grief I didn't have words for. Feel free to use that, but I want the essay to go beyond my story.
Argue that the best software in the world is boring internal tooling nobody outside the company ever sees.
Why do some sports get more beautiful in slow motion and others just look weird? Essay exploring what that says about the kinds of movement we find graceful.

My partner reads every terms of service agreement before clicking accept. Every single one. Takes him like 40 minutes for some apps. I used to think it was ridiculous but now I'm starting to think he's the only sane one. Can you write an essay about consent and the click-through agreement, like is it even consent if nobody could possibly read them all?
Essay arguing that walking is the most underrated exercise.

Please write an essay considering whether digital photographs will survive as long as printed ones. I have 47,000 photos on my phone and almost none of my grandmother's generation's photos have been lost.
Write an op-ed arguing that cities should treat public pools as essential infrastructure, like libraries, rather than amenities. Context: our city just closed 3 of its 7 outdoor pools citing budget.
what's lost when GPS means you never get lost? would love a short essay, nothing too heavy

My grandfather boxed in the Navy and never talked about it except to say it taught him how to get hit. I keep coming back to that phrase. Write an essay about what combat sports teach that other sports can't, and whether "learning how to get hit" is a skill worth having.
Explore why video calls are more exhausting than in-person meetings of the same length. I've seen the eye contact theories, I want something that goes further.
Write an essay ranking nothing, just defending the honor of the sport everyone makes fun of: curling. Earnestly.

Why do old video games feel more like places than new ones, even though new ones are vastly bigger and more detailed? Write me an essay. I'm thinking specifically of something like Ocarina of Time vs. any modern open world game.
